88% of UK tech vacancies right now are permanent roles, not contract.

That number surprises people outside recruitment. It shouldn't surprise anyone inside it.

For two years candidates held the leverage — thin vacancy volumes, cautious employers, nobody wanting to hand in notice. That's shifting.

REC and KPMG's recent report shows permanent placements growing at their strongest pace in four years, while candidate supply is growing at its slowest in three. Fewer people putting themselves on the market, more employers actually committing to headcount.

But candidates are chasing AI, data and cyber skills, not job titles. AI engineer vacancies are up nearly 75% year on year in permanent hiring, and almost doubled in contract roles. Yet overall tech pay growth has barely moved — average advertised salaries are flat year on year.

Which means employers are desperate for AI capability, candidates who have those skills are fully aware of their value, but the pay that hasn't caught up yet.

That gap won't hold. Whoever moves first on comp for genuine AI and data skills will out-hire everyone else chasing the same small pool over the next six months.

If you're still pricing AI roles like generic developer roles, you're losing the good ones to whoever isn't.

Most enterprise AI focuses on understanding what already happened.
But what if an AI agent could reason about what could happen next?
What if demand dropped 20%?
A major customer defaulted?
A supplier failed?
Interest rates increased?
Production capacity declined?
Hiring froze?
Costs suddenly increased?
This is the idea behind Xpert Systems’ Connected Enterprise What-If datasets.
A Connected Enterprise links customers, suppliers, employees, products, contracts, operations, transactions and financial records across time.
The What-If version introduces a scenario or shock and allows its consequences to propagate across the enterprise.
For example:
Supplier Disruption → Procurement → Inventory Shortage → Production/Fulfillment → Customer Impact → Revenue → Cash Flow → Financial Statements
One event can create second- and third-order effects across multiple business processes.
Now the AI agent doesn't simply answer:
What happened?
It must reason:
What happens if conditions change?
Which processes are affected?
What are the downstream consequences?
What happens to revenue, costs, cash and operations?
What actions could management take?
Which decision could produce a better outcome?
This creates environments for AI model training, AI agent training, scenario analysis, counterfactual reasoning, evaluation and benchmarking.
Instead of testing whether an agent can retrieve the correct record, we can test whether it can reason through an enterprise as conditions change.
That is a much harder—and potentially much more valuable—AI problem.
And Connected Enterprises are only part of our strategy.
Xpert Systems also buys and licenses real-world enterprise data that can legally be used for AI training, evaluation, benchmarking and research.
We are interested in legally licensable historical and operational data including:
ERP • CRM • Accounting • Procurement • Manufacturing • Supply Chain • Engineering • HR • Transactions • Contracts • Documents • Emails
Historical data is particularly valuable because it can reveal how real businesses responded when conditions actually changed.
The goal is to move enterprise AI beyond understanding what happened toward reasoning about:
What could happen? Why? What are the consequences? And what should we do next?
Building AI models or AI agents that need enterprise-scale What-If environments?
Or have real enterprise data you have the legal right to license for AI?

The tool has an owner. The decision it influences often doesn’t.

Every enterprise deploying AI in HR can name who procured the platform, who configured it, and who renews the contract.

Fewer can name who answers for the decision it influenced.

Take a routine case. A model ranks applicants. A recruiter reviews the top of the list. A hiring manager makes the offer. Three people touched the outcome. None of them set the model’s criteria, and none can fully explain its weighting.

The gap is structural. Responsibility for the system is divided by function. Procurement holds the vendor. IT holds the integration. HR holds the process. Legal holds the exposure.

Responsibility for the decision falls between them.

Regulators have begun to classify AI used in employment decisions as high-risk. That changes the question an organisation must be able to answer: not whether it uses AI, but who is accountable for what the AI influenced.

Ownership of the tool is a procurement fact. Ownership of the decision is a governance choice.

Until that choice is made, in writing and before an audit or a dispute forces it, accountability sits with whoever is asked first.

So, look, non-competes again. 🇬🇧 AI start-ups say the government's reform "must go further and faster" (MLex, 2 Oct).

I've hired engineers out of big companies, and watched strong candidates lose 6 to 12 months to a clause they signed at 24 (and, lol, I signed my first one at 21!!). And that's just because the employer had a template that included it, and put pressure to sign it.

What I think we should have - Short statutory cap (3 months was proposed in 2023 and never implemented).

The fair counter-argument from hiring companies: employers who invest in training and client relationships need some protection, and a clean ban on non-competes pushes everyone towards more secrecy, and a feeling of USSR inside modern tech firms.

Still, my bet is that mobility drives more growth than restriction could protect.

When did you last read the restrictive covenants in your own employment contract template?

The 2026 skills landscape has a hidden inversion that most career planning frameworks miss. The fastest-growing skills are not the hardest technical ones. They are the human skills that become critical precisely because technical execution is being automated.

I have been studying the convergence of the 2026 talent market data with what I see in production environments. The most non-obvious takeaway is that cross-functional collaboration and mentorship are not soft skills anymore. They are the binding layer that makes autonomous systems safe. When AI agents execute code and make decisions, the human skill of clearly defining intent, constraints, and escalation paths becomes a technical requirement. A team without strong cross-functional collaboration will produce agents that optimize locally, creating systemic risk.

Another structural shift is that adaptability and continuous learning have moved from aspirational attributes to operational necessities. The half-life of a specific tool or framework is now measured in months. The teams that win are not the ones with the most certifications in the latest platform. They are the ones with engineers who can reason about first principles and reconfigure their mental models as the stack evolves. This is not about learning faster; it is about unlearning faster.

The data from the latest market reports confirms a trend I have observed directly: the demand for analytical thinking and business analytics is surging, even for deeply technical roles. The reason is that AI can generate code, but it cannot yet frame the right question. The engineer who can translate a business constraint into a data contract, or a regulatory requirement into a validation rule, is the one who becomes irreplaceable. The role of the practitioner is shifting from executing to defining what correct execution looks like.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to memorize a vendor-specific certification path. I am seeking a problem where I can combine deep technical architecture with the human skills of defining intent, mentoring teams through ambiguity, and translating business constraints into technical guarantees. If your organization is struggling to retain talent because the technical stack changes faster than your team can adapt, or if your autonomous systems are failing because the human communication layer is weak, I want to hear about the specific cross-functional dynamics and learning models you are experimenting with.

What is the one non-technical skill on your team that, if strengthened, would immediately improve your technical delivery velocity?

Most tech companies fail in a new GCC market before they sign a single client.

The problem is their first hire.

It happens to European and US scale ups landing in Dubai. It happens to UAE startups expanding into Saudi too.

The instinct is always the same: hire a big name who ran the region for a global giant. Someone whose calls get returned.

Then 9 months later, there's no pipeline.

What most founders miss is that, here as anywhere, many people return calls to the logo as much as to the person. That network was borrowed from the old employer. When the logo changes, a lot of it goes quiet.

The big name isn't a bad hire. It's a year 3 hire. Once you have local references and a few clients of your own, their network finally has something to sell.

In year 1, you need a builder. Someone who can open doors with no brand behind them and learn how buyers here actually buy, and who really signs.

So measure that first hire differently. A revenue quota in month 1 makes them burn their contacts on quick wins. Judge the first 6 months on what they learn: which accounts are real, how each one buys, who decides.

A simple interview test: ask what they built somewhere nobody knew their company's name. If every story starts with the logo they worked for, keep looking.

And no hire replaces you. Buyers here want to meet the founder, often more than once.

Contacts get you the first meeting. A builder gets you the contract.

Founders who've expanded into or across the Gulf: would you hire the big name in year 1 or year 3?

**When Recruitment Forgets the Human, Everyone Pays the Price.**

Recruitment is often treated as a numbers game.

Applications received. CVs screened. Interviews completed. Time to hire. Cost per hire.

These metrics have their place. But they do not tell the whole story.

What happens when a recruitment process is so complicated that good candidates abandon it?

What happens when applicants receive no meaningful updates, job requirements are unclear, or interview processes stretch across multiple rounds without a clear purpose?

What happens when AI is introduced to make hiring more efficient, but nobody stops to consider whether the experience has actually improved?

You may still be measuring activity.

You may even be reducing administrative time.

But are you identifying the right talent? Are you building trust? Are you protecting your employer brand?

And are you treating the people behind those applications with basic professional respect?

At Iron Key Consultancy, we believe effective HR is not simply about having processes in place. It is about having processes that serve a clear purpose.

A stronger recruitment process should include:

- **Clarity:** Candidates understand the role, requirements, and relevant expectations.
- **Consistency:** Selection criteria and assessment methods are appropriate and applied fairly.
- **Communication:** Applicants receive realistic expectations about timelines and updates.
- **Efficiency:** Every interview, assessment, and approval adds value rather than unnecessary friction.
- **Accountability:** Hiring teams recognize that candidate experience is shaped by their decisions, not just by the recruitment team.

Technology can absolutely support this.

AI can assist with repetitive tasks, improve workflows, and help teams manage information. But technology does not remove the need for human judgment, responsible oversight, or a process designed around the actual hiring objective.

**A process can be automated and still be a bad process.**

And a recruitment process that frustrates qualified candidates, damages trust, or creates unnecessary barriers is not necessarily efficient simply because it uses fewer human hours.

The goal should not be to make recruitment more complicated, more automated, or more impressive on a dashboard.

The goal should be to make it work.

For the business. For the hiring team. And for the people applying.

Because the human side of business begins long before someone signs an employment contract.

It begins with the first interaction.

**Build a better process. Protect the human experience. Hire with intention.**

A cheaper first quote can become a costly project if rework is ignored.

A quote shows the initial cost, but the project can also consume time through rework, delays and supervision. A lower price may be a good choice when the fit and process are sound. It becomes a false saving when you ignore the work required to recover from poor execution or unclear expectations.

A delayed build may require internal staff to coordinate a second provider, redo decisions and postpone a launch. Those are possible costs to investigate, not reasons to reject every lower quote. Ask how the proposed process will manage the relevant risks.

1. Compare proposals against the same brief.
2. Ask about dependencies and review milestones.
3. Check evidence relevant to the project.
4. Consider the time your team will spend managing the work.

The rebuild in this design illustrates a possible hidden cost, rather than a claim that cheaper providers always fail. Evaluate the full delivery context before choosing.

Every second resume crossing my desk right now claims to be a "Senior AI Engineer."

Received 67 today.

Most of them are prompt wrappers.

They know how to call an OpenAI endpoint, tweak a system prompt, and paste a basic LangChain script into production. But the second you press them on how their system actually processes tokens, retrieves context, or manages GPU memory, the interview falls apart.

If you are hiring for real AI engineering, LeetCode puzzles won't save you. We screen candidates with rapid-fire systems trade-offs:

• Retrieval foundations: HNSW for high-scale vector indexing versus BM25 for lexical precision. (Searching 10 million enterprise contracts where finding an exact clause number demands BM25, but understanding contextual intent requires HNSW.)
• Hybrid search: Using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to blend semantic depth with exact keyword matching. (E-commerce search where a customer queries a specific manufacturer SKU alongside conversational text like "lightweight running shoes".)
• Inference bottlenecks: Managing memory bandwidth through KV caching, PagedAttention, and speculative decoding. (Eliminating VRAM fragmentation and slashing time-to-first-token on an agent handling 5,000 concurrent streaming sessions.)
• Architecture internals: Scaled dot-product attention mechanics and SwiGLU activation functions. (Diagnosing memory spikes and gradient stability when fine-tuning open-weights models on internal domain data.)
• Evaluation rigor: Knowing when to use an LLM-as-a-judge versus deterministic retrieval metrics where you do not waste tokens. (Auditing a compliance RAG pipeline where Context Recall and Hit Rate must be mathematically proven before spending thousands of dollars on LLM evaluation calls.)

Anyone can build an AI demo in an afternoon.

Building production systems that handle latency, prevent context rot, and optimize compute without blowing up your burn rate requires real systems engineers.

Stop filtering for who can write an API call. Start filtering for who understands the mechanics beneath it.

“𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐈𝐓 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝.”

Clients ask for four specific things instead. Each one sounds reasonable on its own. Say yes to all four without thinking, and you have given away a very large discount without anyone ever using the word.

1. “You’re using AI now, so pass the savings on.”

Usually written in as a fixed cut to your rate every year. Fair in principle. The problem is applying one number to all the work. AI genuinely speeds up testing, documentation and first-level support. It barely touches design, architecture, or anything that needs a judgement call. So agree the cut work-type by work-type, and fix the starting point in writing on day one.

2. “Let’s benchmark your rates against the market.”

A third party compares your prices with everyone else’s and resets yours to match. The catch is that “the market” now includes firms quoting on the assumption of heavy AI use. Before the exercise starts, agree who you will be compared against and how the comparison will be adjusted. Leave that open and you have agreed in advance to whatever number the benchmarker arrives at.

3. “Share the savings with us.”

Reasonable, as long as three things are true: the starting baseline is agreed and frozen, someone independent measures the result, and there is a floor your price cannot fall below. Without the floor, it is just a discount that takes longer to arrive.

4. “Let’s do two years instead of five.”

Shorter contracts are workable. But the cost of setting the account up — transition, hiring, knowledge transfer — was priced to be recovered over five years. Over two, it isn’t. So either the client funds transition up front, or the term stays as it was, or the price rises to reflect the shorter run. One of those three. Not none of them.

None of these four requests is unfair. What costs money is treating them as one conversation about price, when they are four separate conversations with four different answers.

Which of the four is coming up most on your renewals?

Four people can hold the title Product Manager and share almost none of the same daily work.

The title sounds like one job. It is not.

Growth PM: lives in funnels and experiments. The week is a conversion drop, a test design and a read-out on whether the lift is real.

Platform PM: negotiates APIs with engineering. The customer is another team, and the product is a contract that has to hold up for ten consumers.

AI PM: spends the week on evals and failure cases. Shipping the demo is easy. Deciding what "good enough" means is the job.

B2B PM: sits in customer calls and pricing debates. One enterprise ask can pull the whole roadmap sideways.

Same title, very different work.

That is why job descriptions and interviews so often feel mismatched. A strong growth PM can stall in a platform role, and the reverse is just as true.

If you are hiring or applying, ask what the week actually looks like before comparing titles.

Which type are you?

Operations & SOP Implementation (HR & Finance)

Corporate operational realignment & tightening overheads (AI infra costs vs. payroll vs. operating efficiency)

Most Indian enterprises don't bleed from lack of revenue.

They bleed from operational blind spots.
Yesterday, news broke that several major tech-first enterprises are pausing standard appraisal increments and freezing ad spends because unseen cloud, AI infra, and vendor operating costs surged unchecked over the last two quarters.

When bottom lines take a hit, the immediate corporate reflex is:
 * Freeze hiring.
 * Slash marketing budgets.
 * Pause appraisals.

As COO, here is the unvarnished truth: these are panic band-aids, not operational solutions.

The root issue isn't employee cost.
It’s the lack of Cross-Functional SOP Governance.

Here is what happens inside 8 out of 10 mid-to-large Indian organisations.

 * Operations expands delivery timelines because handoffs between teams are documented only in WhatsApp groups, not locked workflows.

 * Finance reconciles software, infra, and SaaS licenses quarterly instead of monitoring run-rates in real time.

 * HR takes the blame for bloated headcount, when the real problem is three departments independently purchasing duplicate tooling to do the exact same job.

At Dhan Kush, we look at operational resilience through a simple, non-negotiable framework.

1. The 30-Day "Shadow Stack" Audit
Every departmental software tool, micro-vendor, and external retainer must map directly to an active KPI with an identifiable business owner. If a tool doesn't save billable hours or generate measurable revenue within 60 days, it gets retired.

2. SOPs Must Live at the Point of Action
A 60-page PDF on a shared drive isn't an SOP, it's corporate trivia. Real SOP implementation means embedding compliance and validation directly inside daily software tools - checklists that don't allow a task to close unless verification criteria are met.

3. Tying Finance to Daily Ops Handoffs
Cost control cannot be a month-end post-mortem conducted by Accounting. Ops leads must see their unit-level burn rates weekly. Accountability must precede the P&L review, not follow it.
Scaling sustainably across India’s dynamic market doesn't require cutting people or halting innovation.

It requires operational discipline that runs so deep that surprises simply have nowhere to hide.
